extractedItems.title: What counts as the general area?
extractedItems.question: Which of these places is part of the 'general area' in golf?

choices.text: Putting green for a different hole

extractedItems.explanation: The general area includes fairway, semi-rough, rough, and greens or teeing areas not for the hole being played.
extractedItems.imagePrompt: A teenage girl golfer on a fairway, looking at the grass and gesturing to a nearby teeing ground and a different hole's green in the background.
extractedItems.imageAlt: A teen girl golfer on the fairway, with other greens and tee areas visible.

extractedItems.title: Time to look for a lost ball
extractedItems.question: How long do you have to look for your ball before it is classed as lost in golf?
extractedItems.explanation: You have a maximum of 3 minutes to find your ball. After that, it is considered lost.
extractedItems.imagePrompt: A teen boy golfer searching in the rough with a clock showing 3 minutes next to him.
extractedItems.imageAlt: A teen boy golfer looking for a golf ball in long grass with a clock.

extractedItems.title: What if you move your ball while searching?
extractedItems.question: If you accidentally move your ball while searching for it in the rough, what should you do?

choices.text: Leave it where it stopped moving
Put it back as close as possible to the original spot, no penalty
Take a penalty stroke and continue from the new position

extractedItems.explanation: If you move your ball during a search, put it back on its original spot as accurately as you can, without penalty.
extractedItems.imagePrompt: A teen girl golfer using a club to gently move grass to replace her golf ball on the rough.
extractedItems.imageAlt: Teen girl golfer replacing a golf ball in the rough.

extractedItems.title: Identifying your ball
extractedItems.question: When can you pick up your golf ball to check if it is yours?

choices.text: Only if it is on the putting green
If you mark its position first and need to identify it
Never, you must play it as it lies

extractedItems.explanation: If you cannot tell if it's yours, you may mark its position and pick it up for identification.
extractedItems.imagePrompt: A teen boy golfer marking a spot next to a golf ball in the rough and preparing to pick it up to check if it’s his.
extractedItems.imageAlt: Teen boy golfer marking and identifying his ball in the rough.

reviewedItems.title: What counts as the general area?
reviewedItems.question: Which of the following areas is included in the 'general area' according to the Rules of Golf? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Putting green for a different hole

reviewedItems.explanation: The general area is most of the course, including the fairway, semi-rough and rough, and any green or teeing area for a different hole. Bunkers and penalty areas are not part of the general area.
reviewedItems.imagePrompt: A teenage girl golfer on a fairway, pointing towards semi-rough and a green belonging to a different hole, with a visible tee area in the background.
reviewedItems.imageAlt: A teen girl golfer on the fairway, with other greens and tee areas visible.

reviewedItems.title: Time to look for a lost ball
reviewedItems.question: How much time do you have to look for your golf ball before it is considered lost under the Rules of Golf?
reviewedItems.explanation: You have up to 3 minutes to search for your ball. If you don't find it within 3 minutes, it is classed as lost.
reviewedItems.imagePrompt: A teenage girl golfer searching in the rough while a clock beside her shows 3 minutes.
reviewedItems.imageAlt: A teen girl golfer looking for a golf ball in long grass with a clock.

reviewedItems.title: What if you move your ball while searching?
reviewedItems.question: If you accidentally move your ball while searching for it in the rough, what must you do according to the Rules of Golf?

choices.text: Replace it as close as possible to its original spot, with no penalty
Take a penalty stroke and play from where it stops

reviewedItems.explanation: If you move your ball by accident while searching, you must replace it on its original spot without penalty.
reviewedItems.imagePrompt: A teen boy golfer carefully replacing his ball in the rough after accidentally moving it while searching.
reviewedItems.imageAlt: Teen boy golfer replacing a golf ball in the rough.

reviewedItems.title: Identifying your ball
reviewedItems.question: When are you allowed to lift your golf ball to check if it is yours?

choices.text: Only if it is on the putting green
If you first mark its position and need to identify it
Never; you must always play it as it lies

reviewedItems.explanation: If you cannot identify your ball, you may mark its position and lift it anywhere on the course to check – not just on the putting green.
reviewedItems.imagePrompt: A teen boy golfer marking his ball’s position in the rough before picking it up to check if it is his.
reviewedItems.imageAlt: Teen boy golfer marking and identifying his ball in the rough.
